134.title: Rehras at dusk
134.hook: the evening prayer, said as the day's work ends
134.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Rehras Sahib at sunset, at home or in the gurdwara, as the evening part of Nitnem; it opens with So Dar and includes Chaupai and part of Anand Sahib.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Anand Sahib, the song of bliss: joy has come, O my mother. Your line was joy, found. The morning is done. Now the light starts to go.

There's a moment at the end of a workday. You shut the laptop, or clock out, or take off your boots at the door. The bag hits the floor. For a second you're between things: the day's not quite over, the evening hasn't started. It's easy to fill that second with the phone, the news, the next chore. In Sikh practice, that moment belongs to something else. As the sun goes down, someone lights a lamp, or just sits, and the evening prayer begins.
screen: `THE BAG HITS THE FLOOR.` → `BETWEEN DAY AND EVENING.` → `THE EVENING PRAYER BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Rehras Sahib is the Sikh evening bani, said around sunset as the day's work ends. It's a collection, not a single hymn: hymns of the Gurus from the Guru Granth Sahib, then Chaupai, part of Anand Sahib and a few closing verses. So you've met some of it this week. It opens with So Dar, that door, a version of a passage from Japji, and it asks a huge, open question. In paraphrase: what is that door, and what is that home, where you sit and care for all? Then it answers with music. Countless instruments play there; countless singers in countless ragas sing your praise. Wind, water and fire sing; the continents and the worlds sing. At the end of a long day, when your world has shrunk to your inbox and your sore feet, Rehras opens the window as wide as it goes. And the name? Readers explain it more than one way. Some connect it to a word for supplication, a humble petition. Others hear rah, a road, and read it as provisions for the journey. Both fit: a pause for the traveler where the day's road runs out. The hymns return the day to the hukam, the Divine Order that sustains it all. Said at sunset, they can be heard as handing the day back: what you did, what was done to you, set down inside something larger before the night.
screen: `AT SUNSET, AS WORK ENDS.` · `SO DAR — WHAT IS THAT DOOR?` · `THE WHOLE WORLD SINGING.` · `PROVISIONS FOR THE ROAD.` · then, large: `PUT THE DAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: Sit down as if it were dusk, hands resting in your lap, and bring up three things from today or yesterday: one you did, one that happened to you, one still unfinished. As you breathe out, picture setting each one down on a table beside you, not solving it, just putting it down. If you pray, you can hand them over.
Rehras. The Sikh evening prayer, said at sunset as work ends, opening with So Dar: what is that door?
Your line: put the day down. At dusk, the window opens wide. That's day one hundred thirty-four.

135.title: Kirtan Sohila at night
135.hook: five short hymns said before sleep
135.howItsDone: Sikhs recite Kirtan Sohila at night before sleep as the last bani of Nitnem; it is also read at funerals after cremation, and when the Guru Granth Sahib is closed for the night in the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rehras at dusk, the evening prayer that opens with So Dar: what is that door? Your line was put the day down. Tonight, the last door of the day.

What's the last thing you do before you fall asleep? For a lot of people, honestly, it's the phone: one more scroll, one more video, the blue light on the ceiling. Then sleep comes thin. Parents know a better way from the other side. A child's bedtime has a ritual: the bath, the story, the song, the light going off. The same song every night, so the child knows it's safe to let go. Sikhs have a bedtime song of their own.
screen: `ONE MORE SCROLL.` → `A CHILD'S BEDTIME SONG.` → `THE SIKH NIGHT SONG.`

segments.voice: Kirtan Sohila is short: five hymns in the Guru Granth Sahib, three by Guru Nanak, one by Guru Ram Das, one by Guru Arjan. It's the last bani of the Sikh day, said at night before sleep. Sohila means a song of praise, and in Punjab it's also a word for wedding songs. That's a clue. Guru Nanak's first hymn uses wedding pictures. In paraphrase: in the house where the Creator's praises are sung, sing the song of praise and remember the Creator. Then comes a bride whose wedding day has been set, and friends pouring oil on the threshold, the old custom for welcoming a bride, asked to bless her so she may meet her Lord. The bride is the soul. The wedding is the meeting with God. And here's what makes Sohila unusual: that wedding also means death. Sikhs read Kirtan Sohila every night, and at funerals, after a cremation. The same song for sleep and for death. It isn't meant to be grim. Sleep is a small letting go every night. The Gurus picture death, the great letting go, as a wedding day, not a door slamming. Saying Sohila at night rehearses trust: whatever the night holds, the soul is not going somewhere cold. Another of Guru Nanak's hymns in Sohila pictures the whole sky as a platter for God's worship: sun and moon the lamps, the stars the pearls. You're lying down under that sky tonight.

If you pray, let Sohila's first line be there; if not, just let go, the way a child does when the song ends.

136.title: How long it takes
136.hook: the full Nitnem takes an hour or more, and traditions differ slightly on which banis are included
136.howItsDone: A full Nitnem takes an hour or more each day; Sikhs who have taken amrit keep it as part of their vows, while many others and newcomers begin with one bani, such as Japji or Sohila, and add more over time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kirtan Sohila: five hymns for the night, a wedding song said at bedtime and at funerals. Your line was the night song.

Japji, Jaap, the savaiyas, Chaupai, Anand, Rehras, Sohila. You've now met every Nitnem bani, spread from before breakfast to just before sleep. So, the way you'd read a recipe before you start cooking: what does a full day of it actually take? And is everyone doing exactly the same thing? Two plain questions, two plain answers, and neither is meant to scare anyone off.
screen: `SEVEN BANIS SO FAR.` → `READ THE RECIPE FIRST.` → `WHAT DOES IT REALLY TAKE?`

segments.voice: First, the time. The morning banis are the long part: Japji, Jaap, the savaiyas, Chaupai and all of Anand, read at a steady pace, fill most of the hour. Someone who has said them every day for years goes faster. Rehras in the evening is shorter, and Kirtan Sohila at night takes only a few minutes. So a full Nitnem is an hour or more across the day. Second, the differences. Sikhs share the core, but not every detail is the same everywhere. The Rehat Maryada from the Akal Takht lists three morning banis; other Sikhs, especially those who have taken amrit, say five. Some traditions, like the Damdami Taksal and some jathas, recite a longer Rehras or a longer Chaupai. Some Sikhs add more, like Sukhmani or Asa di Var in the morning. These are differences of practice within one faith, not a ranking of who prays properly. Third, the most useful thing. Sikhs who have taken amrit commit to Nitnem as part of their vows. For many others, and certainly for learners, it's normal to grow into it. A child might learn the Mul Mantar first, then Japji's first pauri, then more. An adult coming back to the faith might begin with Japji alone, or Sohila at night. Nobody arrives at the full hour on day one. Nitnem means the daily rule, and its weight is on daily. One bani, said every day, becomes a path worn across a field.

137.title: Your Nitnem, for now
137.hook: a starter Nitnem is an invitation, not a test
137.howItsDone: Amritdhari Sikhs keep the full Nitnem as part of their vows; many other Sikhs and newcomers begin with one bani said daily, such as Japji in the morning or Sohila at night, and add more over time.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bani: a full Nitnem is an hour or more, with small differences between traditions. Your line was start with one.

Two pieces of paper land on a desk. One is a test, face down, with a box for a grade. The other is a card, a name written on the envelope. A daily prayer can look like the first: a full version you either pass or fail, so why start? Today ends ten days on Nitnem, and the point is the second piece of paper. A starter Nitnem is closer to an invitation than a test.
screen: `THE PAPER, FACE DOWN.` → `PASS OR FAIL?` → `AN INVITATION, NOT A TEST.`

segments.voice: Look back at the ten days. Nitnem: the daily discipline, morning, evening, night. Japji Sahib, where Guru Nanak says clever thinking won't get you there. Jaap Sahib's galloping praise of the Timeless. The savaiyas: without love, nothing. Chaupai: keep me. Anand: joy, found. Rehras at dusk: put the day down. Sohila at night: the song for sleep. And yesterday, the honest math. So what's a Nitnem for now? For Sikhs who have taken amrit, the full Nitnem is part of their vows, and they keep it. For everyone else on this path, whether a Sikh coming back to practice, someone learning alongside a Sikh partner, or someone simply curious, the Gurus' own words point to a gentler start. Gurbani often calls the Guru's word amrit, nectar: something offered to drink. And the Granth's very first lines, the Mul Mantar, end with two words: gur prasad, by the Guru's grace. In that reading, the invitation isn't earned. It's given. So a starter Nitnem might be Japji's first pauri each morning, Sohila at night, or Anand's first stanza with your coffee. Whatever it is, it's said daily, at a time that already exists in your day. And when a day slips, you do what you learned on the breath. You come back.

segments.voice: Choose one morning bani, not forever, just for now: Japji's Mul Mantar and first pauri, Jaap's opening, one savaiya, Chaupai's first lines, or Anand's first stanza. Picture tomorrow morning, where you'll be, how long it'll take, what you'll read or play; if you're here to learn rather than to pray, choose one to listen to. Then sit with the choice: it's made.

138.title: Before you go
138.hook: anyone is welcome; cover your head, take off your shoes, bring no tobacco or alcohol
138.howItsDone: Visitors of any faith are welcome in a gurdwara; they cover their heads, remove their shoes, wash their hands, bring no tobacco or alcohol, and sit on the floor in the main hall.

segments.voice: Yesterday, your Nitnem: one bani, daily, an invitation, not a test. Now a new stretch begins, out of the house: the gurdwara.

Where do I stand? What do I touch? What if I do something wrong and everybody notices? Those are the questions of anyone stepping into a stranger's kitchen, or a stranger's place of prayer. Someone curious can drive past a gurdwara for years and never go in, because nobody told them the rules. So before the next week of visiting, here's what to know before you go. And the first thing comes first for a reason. You're allowed in.
screen: `A STRANGER'S KITCHEN.` → `WHAT IF I GET IT WRONG?` → `YOU'RE ALLOWED IN.`

segments.voice: Gurdwara means the door of the Guru, the Guru's gateway. It's the Sikh place of worship, and its doors are open to everyone: Sikhs, people of any other faith, people of none. That openness is written into Sikh history. The Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the Golden Temple, was built with entrances on all four sides, and Sikhs read that as a welcome to people from every direction and every background. It's also set lower than the ground around it, so you step down to enter, which tradition reads as humility. So what do you actually do? A few things, all about respect for the Guru Granth Sahib, present in the main hall. Cover your head: men, women and children all do. A scarf, a bandana, anything that covers the hair; gurdwaras often keep a basket of head coverings by the door. Take off your shoes. There's usually a shoe rack or a room for them, often a place to wash your hands, and sometimes your feet. Bring no tobacco, alcohol or drugs, not even in a pocket: the Sikh code of conduct forbids tobacco and intoxicants, and they don't come into the gurdwara. Dress modestly, and expect to sit on the floor. That's it. Nobody will ask what you believe, or ask you to join anything. If you're unsure what to do next, ask, and someone will usually show you, often with a plate of food to follow. Hospitality is part of what a gurdwara is for.

139.title: Am I Sikh enough?
139.hook: cut hair, no amrit, no Punjabi: the Sikh code defines a Sikh by belief, and the gurdwara door is open at every stage
139.howItsDone: The Sikh Rehat Maryada defines a Sikh by belief; gurdwaras welcome anyone who covers their head and removes their shoes, and Sikhs live their Sikhi at many stages, from first visit to amrit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gurdwara, the door of the Guru: head covered, shoes off, and you're in. Your line was everyone is welcome. Today, the question some people carry to that door and never say out loud. Day one hundred thirty-nine.

A car in a gurdwara parking lot. The engine's off, and nobody gets out. Inside, a young man with short hair is running through a list. My grandfather wore a turban; I don't. I can't read Gurmukhi. I haven't been here since I was a kid. Will people look at me? Am I even allowed to call myself Sikh? A lot of people sit in that car. Some sit there for years. Today, the question, and an honest answer.
screen: `A CAR IN THE PARKING LOT.` → `SHORT HAIR. NO GURMUKHI. YEARS AWAY.` → `AM I SIKH ENOUGH?`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Sikh means learner, and a learner, by definition, isn't finished. Then the code. The Sikh Rehat Maryada, the code of conduct most gurdwaras follow, defines a Sikh first by belief: in one God, the ten Gurus, the Guru Granth Sahib and the Gurus' teaching, and the tenth Guru's amrit, with allegiance to no other religion. It doesn't open with a haircut or a language test. Uncut hair does matter deeply in Sikhi. It's a vow for those who take amrit, and many Sikhs hold that every Sikh should aim to keep it. Sikhs differ, sometimes strongly, on how that applies to someone who isn't there yet. That's a real conversation, and your Keeper is a good person to have it with. What isn't in doubt is the door. Langar feeds whoever sits down. Cover your head, take off your shoes, and you're in. Many Sikhs answer this exact worry with an old saying: the house of Nanak is open to all. And not reading Gurmukhi? Plenty of Sikhs, especially those who grew up far from Punjab, are in exactly that spot, and many learn as adults. So the useful question isn't, am I Sikh enough? It's the learner's question: what's my next step? For one person it's walking in. For another, one bani, or one letter. That's Sikhi: the Sikh way, a path you walk, not a badge you earn before you start.

140.title: Bowing to the word
140.hook: people bow before the Guru Granth Sahib and may leave an offering
140.howItsDone: On entering the main hall of a gurdwara, Sikhs walk up to the Guru Granth Sahib, may place an offering of money or food, and kneel to touch their forehead to the floor before sitting with the sangat; visitors are welcome to bow or simply sit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sikhi, and a question asked in a parked car. Your line was start where you are. This week: Rehras at dusk, Sohila at night, bani, your Nitnem, gurdwara, and the open door. Today, through it.
screen: `REHRAS · SOHILA · BANI · YOUR NITNEM · GURDWARA · THE OPEN DOOR.`

segments.voice: You've left your shoes at the rack. Your head is covered. You step into the main hall, the darbar, and it's bigger and brighter than you expected. Carpets or white sheets cover the floor. People sit cross-legged. Harmonium, tabla, voices singing. And at the far end, raised up under a canopy, wrapped in beautiful cloth, is a book. One by one, people walk up the middle of the room toward it, kneel, and touch their foreheads to the floor. What are they doing, and what are they bowing to?
screen: `THE DARBAR, BRIGHT AND OPEN.` → `A BOOK UNDER A CANOPY.` → `FOREHEADS TO THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: It's called matha tekna. Matha is the forehead; tekna means to rest, to lean it down. Resting your forehead before the Guru. And the Guru here is the Guru Granth Sahib. Sikh tradition tells that in 1708, before he died, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, declared there would be no more human Gurus after him. The Guru would be the word itself, the scripture, alongside the community, the Khalsa Panth. So Sikhs bowing in the gurdwara aren't bowing to paper and ink, and not to an idol. They're bowing to the Guru's word, the living teacher, present in the room. How it's done: people walk slowly up the central aisle, often with hands folded. Many place an offering before the Granth: money in the box called the golak, food for the langar kitchen, or nothing at all. Then they kneel, touch their forehead to the floor, step back and sit among the sangat, usually taking care not to sit with their feet or back toward the Guru Granth Sahib. The offering isn't a fee. The gurdwara runs on the community's giving, and the golak pays for the langar and the building, but nobody checks what you gave. Visitors aren't required to bow. Many do, as a sign of respect, the way you'd stand when someone honored walks into a room. Others simply sit quietly, and that's fine too. The point is the humility. The head, raised all day, goes down before a word bigger than any of us.
screen: `MATHA — FOREHEAD. TEKNA — TO REST.` · `1708: THE WORD BECOMES GURU.` · `THE AISLE, THE GOLAK, THE BOW.` · `THE HEAD GOES DOWN.` · then, large: `BOW TO THE WORD.`

segments.voice: If you're able, kneel and rest your forehead on the floor, on your folded hands or on a table in front of you; if kneeling isn't possible, just lower your head, and stay there for a few breaths. Notice what it feels like to put the head, the busiest part of you, lower than your heart. If you pray, bow to the Guru's word; if not, bow to whatever you owe gratitude today, then sit up slowly.
Matha tekna. Resting the forehead to the floor before the Guru Granth Sahib: bowing to the word, not to paper.
Your line: bow to the word. The head goes down; the word stays high. One hundred forty days, and counting.

screen: `DAY 140 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: THE CANOPY AND THE WHISK.`
